newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street looks ready for Fed interest-rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street looks ready for Fed interest-rate hike.

text.p: The day before a key Federal Reserve policy meeting, Wall Street staged a powerful rally despite the likelihood of the first interest rate hike in more than two years.
The Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee will hold a one-day meeting Tuesday to decide whether to raise rates to help sustain moderate economic growth.

In several appearances before Congress this year, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has suggested a rate hike would be a timely move to counter potential inflationary pressures that are expected to emerge late this year or early next.

The latest batch of economic reports strengthened the argument for a pre-emptive move by the Fed to slow economic growth. Last week, the Commerce Department reported that builders broke ground on new homes and apartments in February at the fastest clip in nearly three years.

Stock and bond markets have sold off over the past few weeks in response to comments from Greenspan and other Fed officials. By now, the markets seem to have conditioned themselves to an interest rate boost.
Greenspan has repeatedly warned of the inflationary risks posed by tight labour markets while acknowledging that so far prices have remained well under control.

The clearest evidence that the markets already have taken into account a Fed rate hike, which would be the first increase since 1994, is that rates for short-term Treasury bills -- which are the most sensitive to official short-term interest rate moves -- were unchanged on Monday.

Short-term bill rates have risen from 5.02 percent on Feb. 25 -- one a day before the Wall Street heard Greenspan deliver his semi-annual Congressional testimony in a decidedly hawkish tone -- to 5.26 percent on Monday, which was unchanged from Friday's close.

"The fact that those rates have risen lately -- and pretty dramatically after Greenspan spoke last week -- certainly indicates that any people doubting that there would be a rate increase are not doubting any more," said Anthony O'Bryan, vice president at A.G. Edwards & Sons.

The Federal funds rate, a benchmark for other short-term rates that is the Fed's main lever for influencing the economy, now stands at 5.25 percent. Most of those forecasting a rate rate rise look for a modest increase of a quarter percentage point in the Fed funds rate, which is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.
The last time the Fed raised rates was in February 1995, when it completed the last of a series of increases that resulted in a doubling of the funds rate over a year.
O'Bryan said financial markets "will rally after the (Fed rate hike) announcement (expected Tuesday afternoon) and might even rally ahead of it.

"No. 1, it was an uncertainty that the market was dealing with and now it's gone," he said. "And at least from the point of view of bond investors, it would mean that Alan Greenspan is keeping his reputation as an inflation fighter and that should help the long-end of the curve."

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 17/32, or $5.31 on a $1,000 bond Monday, sending its yield down to 6.92 percent from 6.97 percent on Friday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Last week, the long-term rate jumped to the key 7 percent level for the first time since September of 1996. At that level, investors often begin to buy bonds instead of stocks.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 100.46 points at 6,905.25, recovering from a four-session string of losses that wiped 150 points off the blue-chip index. It was the biggest gain for the Dow since Feb. 12, when it rose more than 103 points.
Foreign exchange markets also were adjusting to the idea of an interest rate increase, debating only when the next hike might come.
"The rate hike should be supportive for the dollar," said O'Bryan. "The dollar doesn't need any help, but the higher rates will help anyway."

Much of the financial markets' reaction to a rate hike on Tuesday would depend on whether investors believe the increase is the first of many rate increases, the first of two or three such moves, or just a single move, analysts said.

"Most people will conclude that it's the first of two moves and some are hedging in the direction of another rate tightening (at the next FOMC meeting) on May 20," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
